newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends mixed in US after Greenspan, Rubin remarks.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends mixed in US after Greenspan, Rubin remarks.

text.p: The dollar closed mixed and its broad rally paused as traders prepared for and then digested Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments.

The dollar fell to 1.6165 marks and 117.55 yen in overseas trade before Greenspan's comments put a floor under the decline. Later in the morning, supportive remarks by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin gave dollar/mark a boost.

Rubin's statements that the strong dollar is in the U.S. economic interest and that he was not concerned about the effect of the strong dollar on the U.S. trade deficit were really referring to the dollar/yen, traders said.
However, his comments seemed to boost the dollar more against the mark, they noted.
"Everybody is very skeptical about buying at these high levels, especially against the yen, said Stephen Flanagan, a vice president at Credit Agricole in New York.
The dollar ended at 1.6294/99 marks, up from 1.6220/25 at the open, but it eased to 117.89/94 yen from 118.00/05 yen.
The dollar's rally versus the yen since the beginning of 1997 has been fueled by Japan's weak economy, low interest rates and especially it's tumbling stock market, experts said.
Despite loud protests by Japanese officials this year, the market has continued to sell yen, although with increasing caution, because the signals from Japan and the U.S. seem mixed.

For example, in Tokyo on Tuesday a remark by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto that the yen's weakness was not excessive seemed directly at odds with comments earlier in the day from Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka.
Mitsuzuka continues to warn against excessive yen weakness. The conflicting comments helped deprive the dollar of direction versus the yen, traders said.
"You are going to run into some comments but overall the trend is still higher," said James Powers, a vice president at Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale in New York.
"In the long-run these comments won't have much (impact) unless you back it up with something, intervention-wise," Powers added.

In overseas trade, the dollar backed away from 31-month highs against the mark and a 46-month top versus the yen set on Monday as the market braced for the Fed chief's speech before the Senate Budget Committee on Tuesday.

Although Greenspan warned of the risks of wage-driven inflation in the future, his upbeat assessment of the U.S. economy buoyed U.S. stock and bond markets. Traders had feared a sell-off in U.S. assets could have hurt the dollar.

The market was especially sensitive to Greenspan's comments after the Fed chief spoke in early December about "irrational exuberance" in the U.S. asset markets, which jolted stocks, bonds as well as the dollar at that time.

"(U.S. asset markets) had an early selloff in anticipaton of Greenspan," said John Barlow, senior dealer at Bayerische Landesbank Girozentrale. "He didn't say anything too exciting except that the economy is rolling along. That should continue to underpin the dollar."

Elsewhere, the dollar closed at 1.4190/00 Swiss francs, up from 1.4135/45 francs at the open. It fell to Canadian $1.3365/70 from C$1.3383/88. The pound ended off at $1.6632/42, compared to $1.6642/52. The Australian dollar fell to $0.7775/80 from $0.7781/86.
